title: LRU and LFU Cache
tagline: O(1) get and put with smart eviction — LRU via hashmap + doubly linked list, LFU adding a frequency layer.

sections.content:
Every piece of software that cares about speed eventually runs into the same wall: the data you need most is stored somewhere slow, and fetching it every time kills performance. The solution is a **cache** — a small, fast store that keeps a subset of your data close at hand. The hard part is not building the fast store; it is deciding what to keep and what to throw away when the store is full. That decision is the **eviction policy**, and it sits at the heart of some of the most important engineering in modern systems.

Two eviction policies dominate both real-world engineering and technical interviews: **LRU (Least Recently Used)** and **LFU (Least Frequently Used)**. LRU discards the item that has gone the longest without being touched. The philosophy is **temporal locality** — if you accessed something a moment ago, you are likely to access it again soon; if you have not touched it in a while, it is probably safe to drop. LFU discards the item that has been accessed the fewest total times. The philosophy is **frequency stability** — items that are genuinely popular should stay; items that happened to be accessed recently but are rarely needed overall should go.

Both sound simple as policies. The engineering challenge is implementing them at **O(1) time for every operation** — both reads and writes. A cache that takes O(log n) or O(n) to update is nearly useless in practice; the overhead erases the benefit of caching. Achieving genuine O(1) for LRU requires combining two data structures in a non-obvious way. LFU raises the bar further, demanding a third layer of bookkeeping. This chapter walks through both designs in full depth: the intuition, the data structures, the implementation, the edge cases, and the real-world systems where each policy lives.

By the end you will be able to implement both caches from scratch, explain why every design decision was made, identify when one policy beats the other, and recognise the fingerprint of these algorithms in production systems like Redis, CPU caches, and database buffer pools.

flowchart TD
  A["Cache request for key K"]
  A --> B{"K in cache?"}
  B -- "HIT" --> C["Return value\nupdate recency/freq"]
  B -- "MISS" --> D["Fetch from slow store"]

sections.title: The Whiteboard, the Sticky-Note Stack, and the Tally Sheet
sections.content:
Picture a busy chef's workstation. There is space for only five ingredients on the counter at any time; everything else is in the walk-in fridge. Each time the chef grabs an ingredient, they move it to the front of the counter (most accessible spot). When the counter is full and a new ingredient is needed, the chef returns whatever is furthest back — the ingredient that has been sitting untouched the longest. That is **LRU**: recency determines what stays.

Now imagine a different chef who keeps a tally sheet on the wall. Every time an ingredient is used, they mark a tick next to it. When the counter is full, they return whichever ingredient has the fewest ticks — it is clearly not in demand. If two ingredients are tied on ticks, they return the one that has been sitting there longer (LRU as a tiebreaker). That is **LFU**: frequency, with recency as a tiebreaker.

The first chef needs a way to know instantly which ingredient is furthest back without checking every position. That is the **doubly linked list**: the order of positions is always maintained, and moving an item to the front takes constant time because you only update neighbouring pointers. The **hash map** is the label system that lets the chef jump directly to any ingredient's position without scanning the counter.

The second chef needs all of that plus the tally sheet itself — a structure that groups ingredients by tick count and can instantly find both the minimum-tick group and the oldest item within that group. Every data structure decision in these cache implementations maps directly to a real bookkeeping task.

sections.title: Why O(1) Demands Two Data Structures for LRU
sections.content:
The naive LRU implementation most people first imagine is an ordered list: on every access, find the item and move it to the front; on eviction, remove from the back. This works logically but fails on performance.

With a plain array or linked list, **finding** the item by key requires scanning from the front — O(n). With a hash map alone you get O(1) lookup, but the map has no concept of order; you cannot determine which item is least recently used without additional bookkeeping.

The insight is that these two requirements are complementary and neither structure can satisfy both:
- **Hash map**: O(1) lookup by key, no ordering.
- **Doubly linked list**: O(1) insertion at head, O(1) removal from any position (given a pointer to the node), maintains order. But O(n) lookup by key.

Combining them gives the best of both worlds. The hash map stores `key → node_pointer`. The doubly linked list stores nodes in recency order (head = MRU, tail = LRU). When you access a key:
1. Look up the node pointer in the map — O(1).
2. Use the pointer to directly remove the node from its current list position — O(1) because you have the node itself and a doubly linked list lets you update `node.prev.next` and `node.next.prev`.
3. Re-insert the node at the head — O(1).

Why doubly and not singly linked? With a **singly linked list**, to remove a node you need its predecessor (to update `predecessor.next`). But the node only knows its successor, not its predecessor. Finding the predecessor requires O(n) traversal. A doubly linked list stores `prev` and `next` in every node, so removing any node is two pointer reassignments — truly O(1).

Eviction is then trivial: the tail sentinel's `prev` is always the LRU node. Remove it, delete from the map, done — O(1).

sections.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  H["HashMap\nkey -> node ptr"]
  H -.->|"O(1) lookup"| N2["node B"]
  DH["dummy HEAD\n(MRU sentinel)"]
  DH --> NA["node A\n(most recent)"]
  NA --> N2
  N2 --> N3["node C"]
  N3 --> DT["dummy TAIL\n(LRU sentinel)"]
  DT -.->|"tail.prev = LRU"| N3
sections.caption: LRU internals: the HashMap gives direct O(1) access to any node by key. The doubly linked list maintains recency order. Dummy head and tail sentinels mean every real node always has non-null prev and next pointers — no edge-case code needed.

sections.title: The Sentinel Node Pattern — Eliminating Edge Cases
sections.content:
A subtle but important implementation detail: every production LRU cache uses **dummy sentinel nodes** at the head and tail of the doubly linked list. Why does this matter so much?

Consider what happens without sentinels when inserting the very first node into an empty list. You would need to handle the case where `head` is null — set `head = newNode`, `tail = newNode`, `newNode.prev = null`, `newNode.next = null`. When removing the last node, you set `head = null`, `tail = null`. These special cases pollute every insert and remove function with null-checks.

With sentinel nodes, `head` and `tail` are permanent dummy nodes that never hold real data. They are created in the constructor and live forever. The real nodes live between them. Inserting at the front means: `newNode.next = head.next; newNode.prev = head; head.next.prev = newNode; head.next = newNode;` — four pointer assignments, no null checks, identical code whether the cache has 0 or 1000 real nodes. Removing any real node is always: `node.prev.next = node.next; node.next.prev = node.prev;` — two assignments, guaranteed non-null because sentinels are always there.

This pattern generalises: **sentinel nodes are a standard technique** in doubly linked list implementations to simplify boundary logic. You will see it in language standard libraries (C++ `std::list`, Java `LinkedList`) and in every clean LRU cache implementation in interview settings.

stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Empty
  Empty --> HasItems: put(key,val)\ncap not reached
  HasItems --> HasItems: get(key) hit\nmove node to HEAD
  HasItems --> HasItems: get(key) miss\nreturn -1
  HasItems --> Full: size reaches capacity
  Full --> Full: get(key) hit\nmove node to HEAD
  Full --> Full: put(new key)\nevict TAIL.prev\ninsert at HEAD
  Full --> HasItems: after eviction\nif cap=1
sections.caption: LRU cache state transitions. The key invariant: after every get or put, the accessed node is always at the HEAD. The TAIL.prev is always the eviction candidate.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: Every get and put is exactly: one Map lookup or insert (O(1)), plus at most two calls to #remove and #insertFront (each O(1) — four pointer reassignments total). The eviction on a full cache is O(1) because this.#tail.prev is always the LRU node. The Map stores the actual node object reference, not a copy, so pointer manipulation from the list side is immediately visible through the Map.

sections.title: Tracing Through get and put Step by Step
sections.content:
Let us trace through a concrete sequence to make the pointer mechanics completely explicit. Suppose capacity = 2 and we run `put(1, 'X')`, `put(2, 'Y')`, `get(1)`, `put(3, 'Z')`.

**After put(1, 'X')**: Map: `{1 -> nodeA}`. List: `HEAD <-> nodeA <-> TAIL`. nodeA.val = 'X'.

**After put(2, 'Y')**: Map: `{1 -> nodeA, 2 -> nodeB}`. List: `HEAD <-> nodeB <-> nodeA <-> TAIL`. nodeB inserted at front, nodeA moves back. nodeB is MRU, nodeA is LRU.

**get(1)**: Map lookup gives nodeA directly. `#remove(nodeA)` — sets `nodeB.next = TAIL` and `TAIL.prev = nodeB`. Then `#insertFront(nodeA)` — sets `nodeA.next = nodeB`, `nodeA.prev = HEAD`, `HEAD.next = nodeA`, `nodeB.prev = nodeA`. List: `HEAD <-> nodeA <-> nodeB <-> TAIL`. nodeA is now MRU. Returns 'X'.

**put(3, 'Z')**: Cache is full (size = 2). LRU = `this.#tail.prev` = nodeB (key=2). `#remove(nodeB)` — splices nodeB out. `this.#map.delete(2)` — removes key 2 from map. Create nodeC, `#insertFront(nodeC)`. List: `HEAD <-> nodeC <-> nodeA <-> TAIL`. Map: `{1 -> nodeA, 3 -> nodeC}`.

Notice: get(2) now returns -1 because key 2 was evicted. The node for key 1 (nodeA) survived because it was accessed in the get(1) step, making key 2 the LRU candidate.

This trace reveals the critical invariant: **the order in the doubly linked list always matches the access timeline**. MRU at head, LRU at tail, and every operation maintains this invariant in O(1) time.

sections.title: LFU: Adding the Frequency Dimension
sections.content:
LRU is elegant but has one weakness: it is myopic about history. If a hot item was not accessed in the last 60 seconds but is accessed thousands of times per hour, LRU might evict it during a cold gap. **LFU** solves this by tracking the **total access count** of every item over its lifetime in the cache.

The naive LFU implementation is straightforward: keep a `(key, frequency)` pair and a min-heap. On access, increment the frequency and sift up in the heap; on eviction, pop the heap minimum. This gives O(log n) per operation — faster than O(n) linear scan but still not O(1).

Achieving O(1) LFU requires a cleverer structure. The key insight is: instead of sorting items by frequency, **group items by frequency**. Maintain a bucket for each frequency value, containing all items at that frequency. To find the eviction candidate, look up the minimum-frequency bucket. Within a bucket, apply LRU ordering (insertion order) for tie-breaking.

The O(1) LFU uses three components:
1. **`keyMap: Map<key, {value, freq}>`** — O(1) lookup of any key's value and current frequency.
2. **`freqMap: Map<freq, Set<key>>`** — groups keys by their current frequency. `Set` in JavaScript maintains insertion order, giving LRU within each bucket.
3. **`minFreq: number`** — tracks the lowest frequency bucket. Used to find the eviction target without scanning all buckets.

The `minFreq` variable is the most subtle part. It can only be updated in two ways: (a) when a get or put-update increments a key's frequency and the old frequency bucket becomes empty, `minFreq` might need to increase by 1; (b) when a new key is inserted, `minFreq` is always reset to 1 because new keys always start with frequency 1, which is always the minimum.

Critically: incrementing `minFreq` is valid after an access only because the item that was at `minFreq` just moved to `minFreq + 1`. If the old bucket is now empty, the new minimum is `minFreq + 1`. If the old bucket still has other items, `minFreq` does not change. This logic is captured in the `#incrFreq` helper.

flowchart TD
  KM["keyMap\nkey -> value, freq"]
  FM["freqMap\nfreq -> Set of keys"]
  MF["minFreq = 1"]
  FM --> F1["freq=1: Set{C, D}"]
  FM --> F2["freq=2: Set{A}"]
  FM --> F3["freq=5: Set{B}"]
  MF -.->|"evict from here"| F1
  KM -.->|"lookup"| FM
sections.caption: LFU internal state example. keyMap gives O(1) access to any key's frequency. freqMap groups keys by frequency; insertion-ordered Sets give LRU tiebreaking within each bucket. minFreq=1 means the next eviction targets Set{C,D}, removing C (oldest insertion).

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The Set in JavaScript maintains insertion order by specification, and Set.values().next().value retrieves the first-inserted (oldest) element in O(1). This gives each frequency bucket implicit LRU ordering for free. The minFreq variable is reset to 1 on every new-key insertion because new keys always start at frequency 1, which is always the global minimum at that moment.

sections.title: Comparing LRU and LFU: When Each Policy Wins
sections.content:
Understanding when to use each policy is as important as knowing how to implement them. The right choice depends entirely on the **access pattern** of your workload.

**LRU wins for temporal locality workloads.** Web page caches, CPU instruction caches, OS page replacement, and database buffer pools all exhibit temporal locality: recently accessed data is statistically much more likely to be accessed again soon. LRU is a nearly optimal policy for these workloads and is simpler to implement. Redis, Memcached, and most web caches default to LRU.

**LFU wins for stable hot-spot workloads.** Think of a streaming platform where a handful of popular songs are played thousands of times per day. LFU keeps them in cache indefinitely, regardless of momentary cold gaps. A hot song that was not played in the last 10 minutes would survive LFU but might be evicted by LRU.

**LRU beats LFU for sequential scans.** If a process scans a large table or file — accessing each item exactly once — every item enters with frequency 1 and competes equally for LFU eviction. This is called **cache pollution**: the scan displaces genuinely hot items. LRU handles this more gracefully because scan items are immediately the oldest in the cache after they are accessed, making them the first to be evicted when new items arrive.

**LFU has worse cold-start behaviour.** A new, popular key starts at frequency 1. In a cache full of keys with high frequencies, the new popular key will be evicted immediately even if it would become the hottest item in the dataset. LRU treats a new key as the most recently used, giving it time to prove its value.

**LFU suffers from frequency staleness.** A key accessed heavily two hours ago but not since has a high frequency count. If the workload shifts and that key is no longer needed, LFU will keep it in cache far longer than LRU would. Some variants (LFRU, LFU with aging) decay frequencies over time to address this.

**Practical recommendation**: default to LRU for most web and database caching scenarios. Use LFU only when you have measured evidence that your hot-item set is stable over long time periods and that hot items are being displaced by LRU during cold gaps.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  WL["Workload Type"]
  WL --> TL["Temporal Locality\nrecent = likely reused"]
  WL --> HS["Stable Hot Spots\nsome keys always popular"]
  WL --> SS["Sequential Scan\neach key accessed once"]
  TL --> LRU1["LRU wins"]
  HS --> LFU1["LFU wins"]
  SS --> LRU2["LRU wins\nLFU polluted by freq=1"]
sections.caption: Policy selection by workload type. LRU is the safe default. LFU is better only when the hot-item set is stable over long periods and cold-gap evictions are measured to be a real problem.

sections.title: Real-World Systems Using These Policies
sections.content:
Cache eviction policies are not academic — they are configured choices in production systems you will encounter as an engineer.

**Redis** supports six eviction policies via `maxmemory-policy`: `allkeys-lru` (evict any key by LRU), `volatile-lru` (evict only keys with a TTL by LRU), `allkeys-lfu` (evict any key by LFU, added in Redis 4.0), `volatile-lfu`, `allkeys-random`, and `noeviction` (return errors when full). Redis implements LRU and LFU approximately — sampling a random subset of keys and evicting the best candidate among the sample — because maintaining a true global ordering would be too expensive.

**CPU caches (L1/L2/L3)** use hardware LRU approximations in their cache-line replacement policies. The sets in a CPU cache are small enough (4–16 ways) that hardware can afford per-set LRU tracking. Modern CPUs often use Pseudo-LRU (PLRU) — a tree of bits that approximates LRU without the full overhead.

**OS page replacement** (Linux, Windows) uses variants of Clock (also called Second Chance), which is an efficient LRU approximation. True LRU would require updating timestamps on every memory access — prohibitively expensive at the hardware level.

**Database buffer pools** (PostgreSQL's `pg_buffercache`, InnoDB's buffer pool) use LRU-based replacement with a 'young/old' region split to resist scan pollution — a problem called the *LRU pollution problem* or *sequential flooding*. MySQL InnoDB inserts new pages into the 3/8 point of the LRU list (the 'old sublist'), not the head, so a large sequential scan does not displace frequently accessed pages.

**Content Delivery Networks (CDNs)** like Cloudflare and Fastly implement LFU-influenced policies at the edge, where static assets (images, JS bundles) have stable popularity distributions and need to survive across many request bursts.

Understanding these policies at the implementation level — not just as high-level concepts — allows you to configure and tune these systems intelligently in production.

sections.title: Edge Cases, Common Mistakes, and Interview Traps
sections.content:
These cache implementations have several sharp edges that trip up candidates and engineers alike.

**Capacity = 0**: The LFU `put` method must guard against `this.#cap <= 0`. Without this guard, size checks compare 0 >= 0 and attempt to evict from an empty cache — a null pointer crash. The LRU implementation must also handle capacity = 0 gracefully (some interviewers ask this explicitly).

**Updating an existing key**: Both LRU and LFU have a `put` path for existing keys. For LRU, updating an existing key must also move the node to the MRU position — not just update the value. For LFU, updating must increment the frequency. Forgetting this makes the cache logically incorrect: the old metadata would suggest the item was not recently used/accessed.

**minFreq and the increment-on-empty rule (LFU)**: The `minFreq++` in `#incrFreq` is only valid when an existing key's frequency is being incremented, not when a new key is being inserted. New insertions always reset `minFreq = 1`. If you increment `minFreq` unconditionally during new insertions, you break the eviction pointer.

**LRU eviction of existing key on put update**: When calling `put` on a key already in the LRU cache with a new value, you must move it to MRU. Many implementations correctly handle the 'key not in cache' insert path but forget the 'key already exists' update path, failing on test cases like: `put(1, 1), put(1, 2), put(2, 3), put(3, 4)` — which key is evicted?

**Thread safety**: Neither implementation above is thread-safe. In production, caches must be protected by locks (coarse-grained mutex), or use concurrent data structures (Java's `ConcurrentHashMap` + `ConcurrentLinkedDeque`). Distributed caches (Redis, Memcached) solve this by being single-threaded per core.

**The JavaScript Map shortcut**: JavaScript's `Map` maintains insertion order. You can implement a minimal LRU using only a `Map`: delete-and-re-insert on access to refresh order, evict via `map.keys().next().value` (oldest). This is acceptable in interviews but the doubly-linked-list solution demonstrates deeper systems understanding.

**Historical context:** The concept of least-recently-used replacement was formalised in the late 1960s as part of research into virtual memory systems. Peter Denning's **working set model** (1968) provided the theoretical foundation: programs tend to access a relatively small, stable subset of pages — the working set — at any given time. LRU approximates keeping the working set in memory. The policy was implemented in hardware by IBM for the System/370 in 1970 and has been a standard in operating system memory management ever since. LFU arrived slightly later as researchers noticed that pure recency was insufficient for workloads with long-lived hot items — frequency was needed as a complementary signal.

**Interview and implementation insights to know cold:**
- State the two-data-structure requirement immediately: 'LRU needs a HashMap for O(1) lookup and a doubly linked list for O(1) reordering — neither alone is sufficient.'
- Dummy sentinel nodes are not optional nicety — they eliminate entire classes of null-pointer bugs and are expected in clean interview code.
- For LFU, the `minFreq = 1` reset on new insertions is the most commonly missed line — it is the key to correctness.
- JavaScript's `Map` iterates in insertion order, making a naive LRU possible with just `Map` — but always mention the DLL approach as the canonical solution.
- When asked 'which policy would you use?' always ask about the workload: temporal locality → LRU; stable hot spots → LFU; sequential scans → LRU (LFU gets polluted).
- Both get and put for LRU and LFU are O(1) **worst case**, not amortised — this is a strong guarantee that makes them practical.

items: **LRU** evicts the least recently accessed item; it is optimal for temporal-locality workloads and is the default policy in Redis, OS page replacement, and CPU caches.

**O(1) LRU** requires combining a **HashMap** (O(1) key lookup) with a **doubly linked list** (O(1) move-to-front and tail removal) — a singly linked list cannot remove an arbitrary node in O(1) because it lacks back-pointers.

**Dummy sentinel head and tail nodes** eliminate null-pointer edge cases in the doubly linked list — every real node always has non-null prev and next, making all insert and remove operations uniform one-liners.

**O(1) LFU** requires three structures: a `key→{value,freq}` map, a `freq→insertion-ordered-Set(keys)` map for bucketing with LRU tiebreaking, and a `minFreq` variable tracking which bucket to evict from.
**minFreq must be reset to 1** on every new-key insertion in LFU, because new keys always start at frequency 1 — the unconditional reset is the most commonly missed correctness requirement.
**LRU beats LFU on sequential scans**: scan items all enter at frequency 1 and pollute LFU by competing equally with hot items; LRU naturally ages scan items out first.

**Production systems approximate** true LRU/LFU: Redis samples random keys and picks the best candidate; OS kernels use Clock/PLRU algorithms; database buffer pools use split-LRU to resist scan pollution.

quiz.question: Why does an O(1) LRU cache require a doubly linked list rather than a singly linked list?
options: Doubly linked lists use less memory and are always faster
Removing a node from the middle of the list requires updating its predecessor's next pointer — available in O(1) only if the node stores a prev pointer
Doubly linked lists support random-access indexing unlike singly linked lists
Singly linked lists cannot support insertion at the head
quiz.explanation: When a node is accessed it must be moved to the MRU head. Splicing it out requires setting predecessor.next = node.next. In a doubly linked list, node.prev gives the predecessor in O(1). In a singly linked list, finding the predecessor requires O(n) traversal from the head.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of dummy head and tail sentinel nodes in an LRU implementation?
options: They store the capacity and current size of the cache as metadata
They eliminate null-pointer checks — every real node always has non-null prev and next, making insert and remove code uniform for all positions
They act as the MRU and LRU items respectively and are returned on get()
They are required to make the HashMap correctly reference nodes
quiz.explanation: Without sentinels, inserting into an empty list or removing the last node requires special-casing null pointers. With dummy head and tail, every real node always has a non-null prev and next (at minimum the sentinels), so the four-line #remove and #insertFront code works identically for caches of size 0 to N.

quiz.question: LRU cache capacity 3, operations: put(1), put(2), put(3), get(1), put(4). Which key is evicted when put(4) is called?
options: Key 1
Key 2
Key 3
Key 4
quiz.explanation: After put(1,2,3) the list is [3,2,1] (3=MRU, 1=LRU). get(1) moves 1 to MRU: list becomes [1,3,2]. The cache is full, so put(4) evicts the LRU tail, which is now key 2. Final state: [4,1,3].

quiz.question: In an O(1) LFU cache, what three components are required?
options: Min-heap, hash map, and a sorted array of frequencies
A key-to-{value,freq} map, a freq-to-ordered-set-of-keys map, and a minFreq variable
Two doubly linked lists and a single hash map
A priority queue, a hash map, and a doubly linked list
quiz.explanation: The key→{value,freq} map gives O(1) value and frequency lookup. The freq→ordered-set map groups keys by frequency and provides O(1) access to the LRU key within any frequency bucket. The minFreq variable tracks which bucket to evict from in O(1) without scanning all frequencies.

quiz.question: Why must minFreq be reset to 1 whenever a new key is inserted in an LFU cache?
options: New keys should always be evicted first to make room for existing hot keys
New keys always start with frequency 1, which is always the current global minimum, so eviction must now target the frequency-1 bucket
Resetting minFreq prevents integer overflow of the frequency counter over time
JavaScript Sets reset their ordering on each Map.set() call
quiz.explanation: A newly inserted key has frequency 1 — the smallest possible frequency value. Since frequency 1 is always less than or equal to any existing key's frequency, the next eviction target must be the frequency-1 bucket. Setting minFreq = 1 guarantees the eviction pointer is correct after every insertion.

quiz.question: Under which access pattern does LFU perform worse than LRU?
options: A stable hot-spot pattern where 10% of keys receive 90% of accesses
A sequential full-table scan where each key is accessed exactly once
A workload where the same 5 keys are accessed in a round-robin loop
A workload where new keys arrive infrequently and old keys dominate access
quiz.explanation: In a sequential scan, every scanned key enters the LFU cache at frequency 1. They all compete equally in the min-frequency bucket, displacing existing hot items that had higher frequencies. LRU handles this better: scanned items become the least recently used immediately after their single access and are evicted first as new items arrive.

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of get and put in a correctly implemented LRU cache?
options: O(log n) due to the need to maintain sorted order
O(1) amortised — fast on average but occasional O(n) eviction passes
O(1) worst case — every operation is a constant number of map lookups and pointer assignments
O(n) worst case when the cache is full and eviction is needed
quiz.explanation: Both get and put are O(1) worst case. get does one Map lookup plus two O(1) pointer operations (#remove, #insertFront). put does one Map lookup, one Map insert/delete, one node allocation, and a constant number of pointer operations. Eviction is O(1) because the LRU node is always at tail.prev.

quiz.question: Which real-world system uses an approximate LRU policy by sampling random keys rather than maintaining a true global LRU order?
options: PostgreSQL's MVCC transaction log — uses FIFO ordering
Redis with maxmemory-policy=allkeys-lru — samples a random subset and evicts the best LRU candidate among the sample
A Bloom filter — uses probabilistic membership, not eviction
Linux ext4 filesystem journal — uses write-ahead log ordering
quiz.explanation: Redis implements approximate LRU by sampling a configurable number of random keys (default 5) and evicting the one with the oldest access time among the sample. This avoids the overhead of maintaining a true global LRU list (which would require updating a pointer on every single read) while approximating LRU behaviour in practice.

quiz.question: In the LFU implementation using JavaScript's Set, why does Set.values().next().value return the LRU key within a frequency bucket?
options: JavaScript Set stores keys in alphabetical order, so the first value is always the lexicographically smallest
JavaScript Set maintains insertion order by specification, so the first value is always the key that was added to that frequency bucket earliest
The .next() method on a Set iterator randomly selects a key for fairness
JavaScript Set sorts numeric keys in ascending order, making the smallest key the first
quiz.explanation: The ECMAScript specification requires Set to maintain insertion order. Within each frequency bucket, keys are added when their frequency increases to that level — so earlier insertions (less recently promoted) appear first. The first value in the Set is the oldest promotion into that bucket, which corresponds to LRU tiebreaking within that frequency level.

quiz.question: What happens in an LFU cache when put() is called for a key that already exists in the cache?
options: The old entry is evicted and a new entry with frequency 1 is inserted at the minimum frequency bucket
The entry's value is updated and its frequency is incremented — it is NOT treated as a new insertion and minFreq is NOT reset to 1
The put() call is ignored because the key already exists
The entry's value is updated but its frequency stays unchanged
quiz.explanation: Updating an existing key in LFU follows the same frequency-increment path as a get(): the value is updated and #incrFreq is called to move the key from its current frequency bucket to the next one. minFreq is NOT reset to 1 — the reset only happens for brand-new insertions. Treating an update as a new insertion would incorrectly drop the key's accumulated frequency history.
